_about: Context for translators and reviewers. 'style' applies to every language, 'languages' to one language, 'prefixes' to every key that starts with that prefix (the longest match wins), 'keys' to one key. tools/lqa.py puts this next to each text in the review page.
style: The app is used by children (about 8 to 14), their parents and teachers. Use short, plain, friendly sentences. Speak to the user directly and informally.
Say what the app does. No marketing language, no exclamation marks unless the English has one.
Keep every placeholder exactly as written, including its case: {0}, {1}, {k}, {S}, {OP} and so on. You may move a placeholder within the sentence when your grammar needs it.

Keep LEGO®, SPIKE™, LDraw™ and their symbols exactly. Never translate or shorten BrickHubRemote, LEGO, SPIKE, Prime, Essential, BrickLink Studio, LDraw, Python, MicroPython, Blockly, Bluetooth, Bluefy, Chrome, Android, iPhone, iPad.
Port letters (A to F), units (cm, mm, ms, %) and key names in the keyboard help (WASD, Shift, H) stay as they are.
Use the words that LEGO® Education uses in your language for the hub, light matrix, motors and sensors where you know them, but not their trademarks or product names beyond the ones listed above.
Button texts must stay short: they sit on small round buttons on a phone. Prefer a short verb over a full sentence.

languages.de: Use 'du' (informal). Use German quotation marks „…“ only if the English has quotes.
languages.fr: Use 'tu' (informal). Put a no-break space before : ; ? ! as usual in French.
languages.es: Use 'tú' (informal), neutral international Spanish (no regional slang).
languages.pl: Use the informal 'ty' form. Mind grammatical case in sentences with placeholders.
languages.zh: Simplified Chinese (mainland). Friendly, simple wording for children; full-width punctuation in sentences.
languages.ja: Use polite です/ます style for sentences and short plain forms on buttons. Use katakana for technical loanwords where that is normal for children.

Settings screen, section 'App' (language, theme, program slot, sounds).
Settings screen, 'About' section. Legal text about trademarks: keep the meaning exact, keep ® and ™.
Settings and Drive screen: extra motors (for a gripper, an arm). 'Hold' = runs while the button is held; 'on/off' = a tap starts or stops it.
Play screen, 'Animation' card: the user draws pictures on the hub's 5x5 light matrix and plays them one after another.
Banner on top of the app when the browser has no Web Bluetooth.
Text on a Blockly block in the Code screen. {A}, {B}, {S}, {P}, {OP}, {F} become small input fields or menus inside the block.
The big connect button at the top of the app.
Building-guide viewer: a 3D model shown step by step (in the Settings screen, robot profile).
Text on a Blockly block in the Code screen (a programming block for children). Each {name} becomes an input field or a menu inside the block, so the text around it must read as one short sentence. Keep it imperative and short, like 'Drive {n} cm'.
Category names in the Blockly toolbox (left edge of the Code screen). One or two words.
Code screen: the block editor (Blockly) and its buttons.
Colour names the colour sensor can see. Short, lower case unless your language capitalises nouns.
Lines in the Log screen while connecting. Technical, for troubleshooting.
Play screen: the user draws a route with a finger on a square area; the robot then drives it.
Error messages in the Log screen and in short pop-up messages.
One-line help text under the connect button, changes with each step of connecting.
Settings screen, 'Hub' section: name, battery, firmware of the connected hub.
Names of the pictures for the 5x5 light matrix (in a menu on a block and in the picture picker).
LDraw colour names, shown in the building guide's parts list. Short.
Settings screen: importing a model file made in BrickLink Studio (LDraw format) to set up the robot's ports.
Settings: how you steer in the Drive screen.
Settings, 'Build a robot': the official LEGO® Education models. Product and model names stay as LEGO® Education names them in your language if you know that name; otherwise keep the English name.
Play screen: buttons that make the robot show a mood with a face on the light matrix and a short sound.
Play screen, 'Move' card: dances and a recorded route that the robot drives.
Messages in the Log screen and short pop-up messages.
Choices in a menu inside a Blockly block (for example 'forward', 'rotations'). Lower case, as short as possible.
Short pop-up message when a game controller is connected or disconnected.
Status pill at the top right: the state of the connection. One or two words.
Example sentences the robot can say in robot language (beeps). Fun, short.
Play screen: a small piano; you can record your own song.
Names of example programs that are added with a robot model.
Code screen in Python mode: an editor for MicroPython that runs on the hub.
A comment inside a line of Python code in the cheat sheet. It appears after '#'. Keep it very short; it is not code.
A comment inside an example Python program (after '#'). Short, plain.
Names of the example Python programs in a menu.
Comments written into Python code that the app generates from the blocks (after '#'). Plain and short.
A window that shows the user's blocks as Python code.
Drive screen and Settings: live sensor values and the obstacle stop.
Settings screen, robot profile (ports, speed, steering).
The share window: a link and QR code to copy a robot profile to another device.
Song titles. All are public domain. Use the title that is common in your language for the same melody; if there is none, keep the English title.
Play screen, 'Robot language': the hub says a typed sentence as beeps.
Sensor values in a menu inside a Blockly block. Keep the unit in brackets.
Tab bar at the bottom of the screen on phones. One short word.
Settings: the robot reacts with sounds when something happens.
Drive screen: steering by tilting the phone.
Settings for robot language: the kind of robot voice.
Labels in a wiring diagram (which motor or sensor goes into which port). Very short.
Settings, language picker and the note about how far a translation is reviewed.

keys.code.stop: Label of the stop button. In capitals in English on purpose: it must stand out.
keys.keys.note: Keyboard help on the Drive screen. Three lines; keep the line breaks and the key names (WASD, Shift, H, Space may be translated if your keyboards say so).
keys.stop.space: Name of the space bar on a keyboard, shown on the STOP button as a hint.
keys.py.hi: A very short greeting that scrolls over the hub's 5x5 lights. Keep it to 2 to 4 plain Latin letters, because the hub's font only has A-Z.
keys.py.hello: Printed by the example program to the hub output. Plain Latin letters only are safest (the hub's console).
keys.code.default: Name of the first, empty program.
keys.profile.default: Name of the first robot profile.
keys.draw.info: {0} = number of straight parts of the route, {1} = total length in cm.
keys.port: {0} is a port letter, A to F.
keys.slot: {0} is a program slot number on the hub, 0 to 19.
